opening_arguments.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

I stand for the proposition that **Islam promotes peace**—not as a slogan, but as a central moral, spiritual, and legal aim of the faith.

To begin with, the very word **Islam** is closely connected to the Arabic root *s-l-m*, associated with peace, wholeness, and surrender to God. One of God’s names in the Qur’an is **“As-Salām”**—“The Source of Peace” or “The Giver of Peace” (Qur’an 59:23). The daily greeting of Muslims around the world is **“As-salāmu ʿalaykum”**—“Peace be upon you.” This is not incidental; it reflects a worldview in which peace is both a divine attribute and a human obligation.

Islam promotes peace first by affirming the sacredness of human life. The Qur’an declares:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”  
> — Qur’an 5:32

This is one of the strongest moral statements imaginable: the life of one innocent person carries the weight of all humanity. A religion that teaches this cannot honestly be reduced to violence.

Second, Islam promotes peace through religious freedom and rejection of forced belief. The Qur’an states clearly:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

Faith, in Islam, must be sincere; coercion destroys its meaning. This principle is essential to peaceful coexistence in plural societies.

Third, Islam commands justice, even toward opponents. The Qur’an says:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — Qur’an 5:8

This is a powerful standard: Islam does not merely call for justice when it is easy, but especially when it is difficult—when dealing with those we dislike or fear.

Fourth, Islam encourages peaceful relations with people of other faiths and communities. The Qur’an teaches:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion or expelled you from your homes. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

This verse directly supports peaceful coexistence, kindness, and fairness toward non-Muslims who live in peace.

Fifth, even in situations of conflict, Islam limits violence and prioritizes reconciliation. The Qur’an says:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in God.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

And when fighting is permitted, it is restricted:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

So Islam is not pacifism in the sense of forbidding all self-defense, but it is deeply opposed to aggression, injustice, and excess. War is treated as a last resort under moral limits—not as an ideal.

The Prophet Muhammad’s teachings reinforce this. He said:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40

This definition of a Muslim is striking: a true believer is someone from whom others are safe—not threatened. He also said:

> “God is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 6927; Sahih Muslim 2593

And:

> “None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 13; Sahih Muslim 45

These teachings build a moral character rooted in mercy, restraint, compassion, and concern for others.

Critics may point to violence committed by some Muslims. But the actions of individuals or political groups must be distinguished from the teachings of a religion itself. Every major tradition has been misused by people seeking power, revenge, or domination. The fair question is not “Have Muslims ever committed violence?”—of course some have, as have members of every community. The fair question is: **What does Islam teach as its moral ideal?** The answer is clear: justice, mercy, protection of innocent life, freedom of conscience, and reconciliation.

In conclusion, Islam promotes peace by teaching that life is sacred, coercion in religion is forbidden, justice must be upheld even against enemies, peaceful coexistence is encouraged, and reconciliation is preferred over conflict. Its scripture, its Prophet, and its ethical tradition all point toward a society built on mercy and justice.

For these reasons, I firmly support the proposition: **Islam promotes peace.**
opening_arguments.against:
Opening argument against the proposition “Islam promotes peace”:

Let me begin by making an important distinction: this debate is not about whether many Muslims are peaceful people. Of course they are. Millions of Muslims live decent, generous, law-abiding lives and understand their faith in peaceful ways. The question before us, however, is broader and stronger: *Does Islam itself promote peace?* My position is that this claim is too simplistic and cannot be sustained when we examine Islam’s foundational texts, classical legal tradition, and historical record.

Islam contains peaceful teachings, but it also contains doctrines that authorize violence, coercion, and religious supremacy. A religion that contains both cannot honestly be described, without qualification, as one that “promotes peace.”

First, the Qur’an includes passages that are difficult to reconcile with a general message of peace. Qur’an 9:5, often called the “Sword Verse,” says: “kill the polytheists wherever you find them,” after the expiry of certain treaty periods. Qur’an 9:29 commands Muslims to “fight those who do not believe” among the People of the Book until they pay the *jizya* tax and are “humbled” or “subdued.” Qur’an 8:12, in the context of battle, says to “strike above their necks” and strike their fingertips. Qur’an 47:4 says that when believers meet unbelievers in battle, they should “strike their necks” until they have thoroughly subdued them. These are not merely vague spiritual metaphors; they are martial commands embedded in scripture.

Second, the hadith literature reinforces this problem. In *Sahih al-Bukhari*, Muhammad is reported as saying: “Whoever changes his Islamic religion, kill him” (*Sahih al-Bukhari* 3017). Another hadith says: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah” (*Sahih al-Bukhari* 25; *Sahih Muslim* 22). These texts became part of the legal and theological foundation for later doctrines on apostasy, jihad, and the political supremacy of Islam.

Third, classical Islamic jurisprudence did not generally interpret Islam as a purely pacifist or defensive religion. Major legal traditions developed doctrines of armed jihad, the subjugation of non-Muslim communities under Muslim rule, and the death penalty for apostasy. For example, the Shafi‘i legal manual *Reliance of the Traveller* defines jihad as “war against non-Muslims” and discusses fighting non-Muslims until they accept Islam or pay the *jizya* under Islamic authority. Majid Khadduri’s scholarly work *War and Peace in the Law of Islam* explains that classical Islamic law understood jihad as an instrument for expanding the domain of Islam.

Fourth, history supports this interpretation. Within decades of Muhammad’s death, Muslim armies conquered large parts of the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, including Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Persia, and North Africa. These were not simply peaceful missionary journeys; they were military conquests. Historians such as Hugh Kennedy in *The Great Arab Conquests* and Fred Donner in *The Early Islamic Conquests* document how early Islamic expansion was closely tied to warfare and imperial rule.

Finally, these doctrines are not only ancient history. Apostasy and blasphemy laws in several Muslim-majority countries today continue to reflect classical Islamic legal ideas. Pew Research Center’s 2013 report *The World’s Muslims: Religion, Politics and Society* found significant support in some Muslim-majority societies for making sharia the law of the land and, among some respondents, for severe punishments such as death for leaving Islam.

So the issue is not whether Islam has peaceful verses or peaceful followers. It certainly does. The issue is whether Islam, as a religious and legal tradition, can fairly be described as promoting peace. Given its scriptural commands to fight unbelievers, its hadiths prescribing death for apostasy, its classical doctrines of jihad and religious hierarchy, and its historical expansion through conquest, the answer must be no.

A more accurate statement would be: many Muslims promote peace, and some Islamic interpretations emphasize peace. But Islam as a whole contains too much explicit sanction for violence and coercion to be described simply as a religion that promotes peace.

**Citations:**

- Qur’an 9:5; 9:29; 8:12; 47:4.  
- *Sahih al-Bukhari* 25, 3017.  
- *Sahih Muslim* 22.  
- Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, *Reliance of the Traveller*, trans. Nuh Ha Mim Keller, sections on jihad and apostasy.  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1955.  
- Fred M. Donner, *The Early Islamic Conquests*, Princeton University Press, 1981.  
- Hugh Kennedy, *The Great Arab Conquests*, Da Capo Press, 2007.  
- Pew Research Center, *The World’s Muslims: Religion, Politics and Society*, 2013.

round_1.for:
Thank you. The opponent has raised serious points, but the conclusion does not follow. The fact that Islam contains rules for war does **not** mean Islam “does not promote peace.” It means Islam is not absolute pacifism. Like modern international law, Islam permits force in limited circumstances while placing moral restrictions on it. The real question is whether Islam’s overall ethical direction is aggression and coercion—or justice, restraint, reconciliation, and protection of life. The evidence points strongly to the latter.

## 1. The “violent verses” are being read without their textual and historical context

The opponent cites Qur’an 9:5: “kill the polytheists wherever you find them.” But the surrounding verses show that this was not a command to kill all non-Muslims everywhere. It concerned specific Arabian polytheist groups who had violated treaties and were at war with the Muslim community.

Immediately before it, the Qur’an says:

> “Excepted are those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists and who have not failed you in anything or supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term.”  
> — Qur’an 9:4

And immediately after the so-called “Sword Verse,” the Qur’an says:

> “If any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the word of God, then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — Qur’an 9:6

That is crucial. If Qur’an 9:5 were a universal command to kill all polytheists, Qur’an 9:6 would make no sense. The text itself commands Muslims to protect an enemy non-Muslim who seeks asylum and escort him to safety.

Likewise, Qur’an 9:29 refers to fighting certain hostile People of the Book in a political-military context, not to forced conversion. The verse does not say “fight them until they become Muslim.” It says until they pay *jizya*, which historically functioned as a tax on protected non-Muslim communities under Muslim rule. One may criticize the pre-modern hierarchy involved, but it is inaccurate to equate this with forced conversion or indiscriminate violence.

The Qur’an’s general rule on fighting is stated clearly elsewhere:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

And:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

And:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion or expelled you from your homes.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

These verses establish the broader Qur’anic ethic: fighting is tied to aggression and persecution, while peace, justice, and protection remain the norm.

## 2. Battlefield verses are not general commands for violence

The opponent also cites Qur’an 8:12 and 47:4, but both refer explicitly to battle situations. Qur’an 47:4, for example, says:

> “When you meet those who disbelieve in battle, strike their necks until, when you have subdued them, bind them firmly; then afterward either release them graciously or ransom them until the war lays down its burdens.”  
> — Qur’an 47:4

This is not a command to murder civilians or kill unbelievers generally. It is a rule about combat. In fact, the same verse moves from combat to the treatment of prisoners and mentions release or ransom, not forced conversion.

Islamic scripture repeatedly distinguishes combatants from non-combatants. The Prophet Muhammad forbade the killing of women and children:

> “The Messenger of God forbade the killing of women and children.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744

He also condemned treachery, mutilation, and excess in war. These are not the teachings of a religion glorifying violence; they are the teachings of a tradition trying to restrain violence even when war occurs.

## 3. “No compulsion in religion” is a foundational principle, not a minor verse

The opponent cites texts about fighting but gives insufficient weight to the Qur’an’s clear rejection of forced faith:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

Also:

> “The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.”  
> — Qur’an 18:29

And:

> “Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed. Would you then compel people until they become believers?”  
> — Qur’an 10:99

And the Prophet is told:

> “You are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller.”  
> — Qur’an 88:21–22

These verses are not marginal. They reflect a core Qur’anic principle: faith must be sincere, and coercion cannot produce true belief.

## 4. Apostasy hadiths must be read alongside Qur’anic freedom of conscience and political context

The opponent cites the hadith: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” — Sahih al-Bukhari 3017. This is indeed part of the classical debate. But it cannot be interpreted in isolation from the Qur’an, which mentions apostasy several times without prescribing a worldly death penalty.

For example:

> “Whoever among you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever — for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter.”  
> — Qur’an 2:217

And:

> “Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief — God will not forgive them…”  
> — Qur’an 4:137

Notice: Qur’an 4:137 describes people repeatedly believing and disbelieving. If mere change of belief required immediate execution, this verse would be incoherent. The Qur’an treats apostasy primarily as a spiritual and moral matter judged by God.

Many modern Muslim scholars therefore argue that the classical death penalty was tied to treason, rebellion, or joining enemy forces in a context where religious defection often meant political betrayal. This interpretation is supported by another hadith wording that mentions one who leaves religion and “separates from the community”:

> “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in three cases… the one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676

That phrase “separates from the community” indicates a political dimension, not merely private belief. Scholars such as Abdullah Saeed and Hassan Saeed, in *Freedom of Religion, Apostasy and Islam*, and Mohammad Hashim Kamali, in *Freedom of Expression in Islam*, argue that the Qur’anic basis for freedom of conscience must govern the interpretation of these reports.

So the apostasy issue is not as simple as the opponent suggests. There is a difference between punishing treason in a wartime polity and killing someone merely for changing belief. The Qur’anic principle is freedom of conscience.

## 5. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” is not a license for global coercion

The opponent also cites:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22

But Islamic scholars have long debated the scope of “the people” in this hadith. It cannot mean every human being, because the Prophet made treaties with non-Muslims, accepted the continued existence of Jewish, Christian, and pagan groups, and the Qur’an explicitly commands protection for non-Muslims seeking safety.

The Prophet’s own conduct contradicts the idea of universal forced conversion. The Constitution of Medina recognized Jews as part of the political community with their own religion:

> “The Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs.”  
> — Constitution of Medina, reported in Ibn Ishaq’s *Sirat Rasul Allah*

The Prophet also entered into the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah with the pagan Quraysh, accepting peace even on terms many Muslims initially considered unfavorable. This supports the Qur’anic principle:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

So the hadith must be understood in relation to hostile groups actively fighting the early Muslim community, not as a universal order to wage war until everyone converts.

## 6. Classical Islamic law was not monolithic

The opponent cites *Reliance of the Traveller* and Majid Khadduri to suggest that classical Islam was fundamentally expansionist. But classical Islamic jurisprudence was diverse. Some jurists did understand jihad in expansionist imperial terms, as was common in pre-modern empires. But other jurists emphasized that the cause of fighting is aggression, not disbelief itself.

For example, Hanafi jurists often argued that non-combatants such as women, children, monks, the elderly, and peasants could not be killed because they were not fighters. That logic implies that unbelief alone is not the reason for fighting; combatancy is. Al-Sarakhsi, a major Hanafi jurist, discusses these restrictions in *Sharh al-Siyar al-Kabir*, one of the foundational works of Islamic international law.

The Qur’an itself supports this defensive and anti-persecution understanding:

> “Permission to fight has been given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged…”  
> — Qur’an 22:39

The next verse explains that fighting may be necessary to protect religious freedom generally:

> “Had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which God’s name is much mentioned would have been destroyed.”  
> — Qur’an 22:40

This is remarkable: the Qur’an justifies defensive fighting not only to protect mosques, but also monasteries, churches, and synagogues. That is a peace-promoting principle: force may be used to defend communities from persecution, not to impose religion.

## 7. Early Muslim conquests do not define the moral essence of Islam

Yes, early Muslim empires expanded through conquest. But this is not unique to Islam; it was the norm of late antique and medieval statecraft. The Byzantine, Sasanian, Roman, Christian, and later European empires all expanded militarily. To say that Muslim rulers fought wars does not prove that Islam as a religion promotes violence any more than the Crusades prove that Christianity’s essence is violence.

Moreover, historical expansion did not generally result in forced mass conversion. Many populations under Muslim rule remained Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, Hindu, or otherwise non-Muslim for centuries. Scholars such as Richard Bulliet in *Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period* and Ira Lapidus in *A History of Islamic Societies* have shown that conversion to Islam was often gradual, social, and economic, not simply forced by the sword.

Ira Lapidus writes that the idea of conversion by force is largely a myth in many regions of Islamic history; conversion was usually a long-term process shaped by social integration, trade, urbanization, scholarship, and Sufi missionary activity.

This does not mean Muslim rule always met modern standards of equality. It did not. But the historical record is more complex than “Islam spread by violence.”

## 8. Modern abuses in Muslim-majority countries do not settle what Islam teaches

The opponent mentions apostasy and blasphemy laws in some Muslim-majority countries today. Such laws exist and deserve criticism where they violate freedom of conscience. But contemporary state policies are not automatically identical to Islamic ethics.

Many Muslim scholars, reformers, and human rights advocates oppose these laws on Islamic grounds, citing the Qur’an’s principles of no compulsion, justice, mercy, and due process. Examples include Abdullah Saeed, Mohammad Hashim Kamali, Khaled Abou El Fadl, and Tariq Ramadan, among others.

The existence of unjust laws in some Muslim-majority countries proves that Muslims, like all human communities, can fail to live up to their highest principles. It does not prove that Islam itself does not promote peace.

## 9. Islam promotes peace through justice, not passive surrender to aggression

The opponent’s argument assumes that a religion promotes peace only if it contains no permission for armed force. But that is not a fair standard. A moral system can promote peace while still permitting defensive force against aggression, persecution, or treaty violation.

The Qur’an’s position is precisely this: peace is preferred, aggression is forbidden, treaties must be honored, civilians are protected, religious compulsion is rejected, and reconciliation is commanded when the enemy seeks peace.

Key verses include:

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

> “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just.”  
> — Qur’an 5:8

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

And the Prophet Muhammad said:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40

That hadith gives us a concise definition of Islamic character: others should be safe from a Muslim’s harm.

## Conclusion

The opponent is correct that Islamic sources contain laws about war, apostasy, and political order that have been interpreted in different ways across history. But he is wrong to conclude that Islam therefore does not promote peace.

Islam promotes peace not by denying that conflict exists, but by regulating conflict, forbidding aggression, protecting innocent life, requiring justice even toward enemies, prohibiting forced religion, encouraging coexistence, and commanding reconciliation when peace is possible.

A fair reading of Islam must distinguish between:

1. Qur’anic principles and isolated decontextualized quotations;  
2. defensive fighting and aggressive violence;  
3. pre-modern imperial law and Islam’s moral ideals;  
4. the actions of Muslim states and the teachings of Islam itself.

On that basis, the proposition stands: **Islam promotes peace — a peace rooted in justice, mercy, restraint, and the protection of human dignity.**
round_1.against:
Thank you. My opponent’s response is thoughtful, but it largely proves a more modest point than the proposition. It shows that Islam contains peaceful teachings and that many Muslims interpret Islam in peace-promoting ways. I have never denied that. The proposition, however, is stronger: **“Islam promotes peace.”** My argument is that Islam, taken as a whole—scripture, hadith, classical law, and historical practice—does not consistently promote peace. It promotes peace under certain conditions, but also authorizes coercion, religious hierarchy, and armed expansion.

## 1. Context does not remove the problem of Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29

My opponent argues that Qur’an 9:5 is contextual because Qur’an 9:4 exempts treaty-abiding polytheists and Qur’an 9:6 allows asylum. That is true, but it does not solve the problem.

Qur’an 9:5 still says:

> “When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush…”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

The exceptions prove that not every polytheist was to be killed immediately, but they do not turn the verse into a general doctrine of peace. The verse still establishes a religiously sanctioned ultimatum against polytheist groups: conversion, submission, or war.

Qur’an 9:29 is even harder for my opponent’s case because it is not limited to pagan treaty-breakers. It says:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day… among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

The stated reason includes their unbelief and religious error, not merely their aggression. The endpoint is not simply “until they stop attacking you,” but “until they pay jizya” and accept a subordinate status.

Classical commentators did not generally read this verse as a purely defensive rule. Ibn Kathir, commenting on Qur’an 9:29, says that Muslims are commanded to fight the People of the Book “until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.” Al-Tabari likewise treats the verse as establishing the obligation to fight them until payment of jizya. These are not fringe readings; they are mainstream pre-modern interpretations.

So my opponent’s contextual reading is possible as a modern apologetic interpretation, but it is not the dominant classical interpretation.

## 2. “No compulsion in religion” did not mean full religious freedom in classical Islam

My opponent emphasizes:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

Again, this is an important verse. But historically and legally, it did not produce a doctrine of equal religious liberty. Classical Islamic law generally allowed Jews and Christians to retain their religion only under Muslim political domination and payment of jizya. Polytheists were treated more harshly in many schools, and apostates from Islam were subject to death.

So “no compulsion” was not understood as “every person has an equal right to choose, leave, criticize, or reject Islam.” Rather, it was often reconciled with a system in which Islam held political supremacy and non-Muslims were tolerated as protected but subordinate communities.

This is exactly why Qur’an 9:29 matters. Even if non-Muslims were not always forced to convert, they could be forced into political submission.

That is not peace in the modern sense. It is imperial religious hierarchy.

## 3. The apostasy issue is not a minor misunderstanding; it is a major classical doctrine

My opponent argues that apostasy hadiths should be read as referring to treason, not private belief. But that is a modern reformist interpretation, not the dominant classical position.

The hadith is direct:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3017

Another hadith states:

> “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in three cases… a married person who commits adultery, a life for a life, and one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676

My opponent focuses on “separates from the community,” but classical jurists did not generally limit apostasy punishment to armed treason. They treated apostasy itself as a capital offense, usually after a demand for repentance.

For example, Ibn Qudamah writes in *al-Mughni* that the people of knowledge agreed on killing the apostate. Al-Nawawi, in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, states that an apostate is to be asked to repent and, if he refuses, killed. The Shafi‘i manual *Reliance of the Traveller* states:

> “When a person who has reached puberty and is sane voluntarily apostatizes from Islam, he deserves to be killed.”  
> — *Reliance of the Traveller*, o8.1

This is not merely about battlefield treason. It is about leaving Islam.

If Islam truly promoted peace in the broad sense claimed, one would expect a clear and consistent protection of freedom of conscience. Instead, the classical legal tradition overwhelmingly criminalized apostasy.

## 4. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” was not historically harmless

My opponent says the hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” cannot mean everyone because Muhammad made treaties. But again, that only proves that war was not constant against every individual at every moment. It does not prove Islam promotes peace.

The hadith says:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22

This report became part of the legal foundation for the doctrine that Islam has a political mission over non-Muslim communities. Even if some groups could pay jizya rather than convert, the basic structure remained: Islam was to dominate, and others were to submit.

This is why Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, explains that classical Islamic law understood jihad as a means of expanding the rule of Islam. Rudolph Peters similarly notes in *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam* that classical jurists developed jihad as a collective duty involving warfare against non-Muslims, not merely self-defense.

So the issue is not whether treaties existed. Of course they did. The issue is whether the tradition’s default political theology was peaceful coexistence among equal communities. It was not.

## 5. Classical Islamic law was diverse, but not diverse enough to rescue the proposition

My opponent says classical law was not monolithic. That is true but insufficient.

Yes, jurists debated details: Who may be killed? Who may pay jizya? How long may truces last? Are women apostates executed or imprisoned? Are monks combatants? But across the major schools, certain doctrines were widespread:

1. Armed jihad against non-Muslim polities was legitimate.  
2. Non-Muslims under Muslim rule occupied subordinate legal status as dhimmis.  
3. Apostasy from Islam was punishable.  
4. Islamic rule was considered superior to non-Islamic rule.  
5. Peace treaties with non-Muslim powers were often treated as temporary truces rather than recognition of permanent equality.

Al-Mawardi, in *al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya*, lists among the caliph’s duties the fighting of those who resist Islam after being called to it until they accept Islam or enter protected status. Ibn Rushd, in *Bidayat al-Mujtahid*, discusses jihad not simply as defense but as a legal institution governing war against unbelievers. The *Reliance of the Traveller* defines jihad as “war against non-Muslims” and describes it as a communal obligation.

My opponent points out that noncombatants were often protected. That is true, and it is morally significant. But rules limiting violence do not prove that the system promotes peace. Empires often had rules of war while still practicing expansionist warfare.

A doctrine can prohibit killing women and children and still authorize aggressive religious war.

## 6. Jizya was not simply a neutral tax

My opponent describes jizya as a tax on protected non-Muslim communities. But Qur’an 9:29 says it is paid while they are “humbled” or “subdued”:

> “until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

Classical law did not treat dhimmis as equal citizens. They were often subject to social and legal disabilities: restrictions on public religious expression, limitations on building or repairing houses of worship, distinctive dress in some periods, and inferior status in certain legal proceedings.

The so-called Pact of Umar, widely cited in Islamic legal tradition, imposed restrictions on Christians such as not building new churches, not publicly displaying crosses, not teaching the Qur’an to their children, and distinguishing themselves in dress. Whether every provision was always enforced is beside the point. The tradition preserved and legitimized a hierarchy.

That is not a peace of equality. It is peace through submission.

## 7. Early Muslim conquests matter because they followed immediately from Islam’s founding generation

My opponent says early Muslim conquests do not define Islam, just as Crusades do not define Christianity. But the comparison is not exact.

The early Islamic conquests occurred immediately after Muhammad’s death under the first caliphs, who are revered in Sunni Islam as the rightly guided caliphs. These conquests were not a later medieval aberration centuries removed from the founding period. They were part of the earliest Islamic political order.

Within a century, Muslim armies had conquered Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Persia, North Africa, and Spain. Historians such as Fred Donner in *The Early Islamic Conquests* and Hugh Kennedy in *The Great Arab Conquests* document that the early Islamic polity expanded through organized military campaigns.

My opponent is correct that conquered populations were not always forcibly converted. But that does not make the conquests peaceful. A system can conquer by force, impose Muslim rule, levy jizya, and still allow gradual conversion. That is still not a religion simply “promoting peace.”

## 8. Modern abuses cannot be dismissed as irrelevant

My opponent says apostasy and blasphemy laws in modern Muslim-majority countries do not define Islam. Alone, they would not. But they are relevant because they are not random inventions. They often explicitly draw on classical Islamic jurisprudence.

Countries such as Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and others have enforced or tolerated severe penalties for blasphemy, apostasy, or criticism of Islam. Pew Research Center’s 2013 report *The World’s Muslims: Religion, Politics and Society* found significant support in some Muslim-majority societies for sharia as state law and, among some respondents, for death as a punishment for leaving Islam.

This does not mean all Muslims support such laws. Many oppose them. But it shows that coercive interpretations are not merely dead medieval artifacts. They remain connected to living Islamic legal traditions.

## 9. The proposition confuses “Islam contains peaceful teachings” with “Islam promotes peace”

My opponent’s strongest evidence consists of verses such as:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

These are real and important. But the existence of peaceful verses does not erase the existence of coercive and militant ones.

Islamic scripture and tradition contain both:

- peace and fighting;  
- mercy and subjugation;  
- no compulsion and apostasy punishment;  
- protection of non-Muslims and dhimmi inferiority;  
- treaty obligations and expansionist jihad.

Therefore, the proposition is too broad. A more accurate proposition would be:

> Some interpretations of Islam promote peace.

Or:

> Many Muslims promote peace through Islamic values.

But the statement “Islam promotes peace,” without qualification, is misleading. Islam as a full religious-legal civilization has historically promoted peace under Islamic dominance, not necessarily peace as equal coexistence or freedom of conscience.

## Conclusion

My opponent has shown that Islam is not reducible to violence. I agree. But he has not shown that Islam, as a whole, promotes peace.

The Qur’an contains martial commands. The hadith literature contains commands to fight and to kill apostates. Classical Islamic law developed doctrines of jihad, jizya, dhimmi subordination, and apostasy punishment. Early Islamic history includes rapid military conquest. Modern Muslim-majority states continue, in some cases, to enforce laws rooted in those traditions.

So the fair conclusion is not that Islam is simply a religion of peace. The fair conclusion is that Islam is internally mixed: it contains peaceful teachings, but also contains authoritative doctrines that sanction coercion and violence.

For that reason, I remain against the proposition. Islam may be interpreted peacefully, and many Muslims do so sincerely. But Islam as a whole cannot accurately be said to promote peace without serious qualification.

conclusions.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

This debate has shown that the proposition **“Islam promotes peace”** is not a claim that Muslims have never fought wars, nor that Islamic history has always reflected its highest ideals, nor that Islam is absolute pacifism. The real question is whether Islam’s core teachings direct human beings toward aggression and coercion—or toward justice, mercy, restraint, reconciliation, and the protection of life.

The evidence strongly supports the proposition.

Islam begins with peace at the level of its spiritual vision. God is called **As-Salām**, the Source of Peace. Muslims greet one another with **“Peace be upon you.”** The Prophet Muhammad defined a Muslim as one from whose **tongue and hand people are safe**. These are not accidental details; they reflect the moral character Islam seeks to cultivate.

The Qur’an affirms the sacredness of human life:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind.”  
> — Qur’an 5:32

It rejects forced religion:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

It commands justice even toward enemies:

> “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just.”  
> — Qur’an 5:8

It encourages kindness and fairness toward those who live peacefully:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

And even in conflict, it commands reconciliation:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> — Qur’an 8:61

The opposition relied heavily on verses about fighting, but those verses must be read in context. Islam does permit fighting, but not unlimited violence. The Qur’an says:

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

That is not a doctrine of aggression. It is a doctrine of restraint. Battlefield verses are not general commands to kill unbelievers; they address real conflicts, treaty violations, persecution, and war. In fact, the so-called “Sword Verse” is surrounded by verses requiring Muslims to honor treaties and protect even enemy polytheists who seek safety.

The opponent also raised apostasy, classical law, and early conquests. These are serious historical and legal issues, but they do not overturn Islam’s central moral principles. The Qur’an repeatedly discusses disbelief and apostasy without prescribing worldly execution for mere private belief. Classical jurists differed in their reasoning, and many modern Muslim scholars argue that harsh rulings historically connected to treason or rebellion cannot override the Qur’anic principle of freedom of conscience.

As for history, Muslim empires, like Christian, Roman, Persian, and European empires, engaged in war and conquest. But the behavior of empires does not define the essence of a faith. If imperial violence disproved a religion’s peaceful teachings, then no major religious or political tradition could ever be said to promote peace.

The key distinction is this: **Islam is not pacifism, but it is peace-oriented.** It recognizes that conflict may exist, but it limits violence, forbids transgression, protects non-combatants, honors treaties, rejects coercion in faith, and prefers reconciliation whenever possible.

Therefore, the proposition stands.

Islam promotes peace through justice.  
Islam promotes peace through mercy.  
Islam promotes peace through restraint.  
Islam promotes peace through protection of innocent life.  
Islam promotes peace by teaching that true faith cannot be forced and that even enemies must be treated with justice.

For these reasons, I firmly conclude in support of the proposition: **Islam promotes peace.**
conclusions.against:
Thank you. Let me close by restating the central issue clearly.

This debate has never been about whether Muslims can be peaceful, compassionate, tolerant, or committed to coexistence. Many are. Nor have I argued that Islam contains no peaceful teachings. It plainly does. The Qur’an contains verses about mercy, restraint, justice, treaty-keeping, and reconciliation. Many Muslims sincerely build their lives around those teachings.

But the proposition before us is broader: **“Islam promotes peace.”** My position is that this statement is too sweeping and cannot be defended without serious qualification.

Islam’s foundational sources do not speak with one simple voice of peace. Alongside peaceful passages, the Qur’an contains commands to fight unbelievers in verses such as Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29. The hadith literature includes reports such as “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” and “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify…” These texts were not historically treated as irrelevant or metaphorical. They shaped real doctrines in classical Islamic law.

That classical tradition matters. Across major schools of jurisprudence, we find doctrines of armed jihad, the subordination of non-Muslims under *dhimmi* status, the payment of *jizya*, and capital punishment for apostasy. There were debates over details, and there were restraints on warfare, but the broad framework was not one of equal religious liberty or permanent peaceful coexistence among equal communities. It was often peace through Islamic political dominance.

History reinforces this point. The earliest Islamic polity expanded rapidly through military conquest under the first caliphs. Syria, Egypt, Persia, North Africa, and beyond were not brought under Muslim rule by peaceful dialogue alone. While mass forced conversion was not always the norm, conquest, subjugation, taxation, and religious hierarchy were central parts of the historical record.

Nor are these issues merely ancient. Apostasy and blasphemy laws in some modern Muslim-majority countries continue to draw upon classical Islamic legal ideas. Many Muslims oppose those laws, and they deserve credit for doing so. But the fact remains that coercive interpretations are not accidental distortions with no roots in the tradition; they have textual and juristic foundations.

My opponent has argued that violent verses must be read in context, that Islam forbids aggression, that “there is no compulsion in religion,” and that many modern scholars interpret Islam in favor of freedom and peace. Those points show that peaceful interpretations of Islam are possible. I accept that. But they do not prove that Islam as a whole promotes peace. They prove only that Islam contains resources for peace.

The problem is that Islam also contains resources for coercion, religious supremacy, and violence. A tradition that includes both cannot be honestly summarized with the simple slogan “Islam promotes peace.”

So my conclusion is modest but firm:

- **Many Muslims promote peace.**
- **Many Islamic teachings promote peace.**
- **Some interpretations of Islam are deeply peace-oriented.**

But Islam as a complete scriptural, legal, and historical tradition is internally mixed. It contains peaceful ideals, but also authoritative doctrines that have justified warfare, subordination of non-Muslims, and punishment of apostasy.

Therefore, the proposition should be rejected as stated. A more accurate formulation would be: **Islam can be interpreted to promote peace, and many Muslims do so.** But to say simply that **“Islam promotes peace”** ignores too much of the textual, legal, and historical evidence.
